conceptTag: Design membership tiers for a gym
readerTitle: One gym, three tiers, and an empty Tuesday morning
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 헬스장, 식당, 미용실 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 요금제 설계는 고객을 나누는 일이다. 등급은 고객이 스스로 자기 자리를 고르게 하고, 울타리는 싼 가격이 엉뚱한 고객에게 새지 않게 막는다.
misconception: 요금제를 여러 개 만들려면 가격만 다르게 붙이면 된다. 할인은 원하는 사람 누구에게나 주면 된다.

sources.text: 가격 정책의 표준 개념 (Good-better-best 등급 구성, 울타리를 이용한 가격 차별)
모든 수치와 사업장은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 헬스장 요금 $30 / $50 / $90, 비수기 요금 $20(평일 오전 10시~오후 4시), 소프트웨어 요금 $15 / $40 / $120은 계산 근거가 아니라 예시 가격입니다. 카드 사이에서 숫자가 서로 맞는지 다시 확인하세요.
실제 헬스장 업계 통계나 기업 사례는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 '비수기 회원권'이 특정 국가에서 법적으로 문제가 되는 표현인지 확인할 필요는 없지만, 연령 기준 할인 언급은 피했습니다.

cards.title: One gym, one price, two very different members.
body: Maya's neighborhood gym charges everyone $50 a month. One member comes twice a month for the treadmill. Another comes every day, takes three classes a week and borrows a towel each time.
They pay the same. Meanwhile, from 10am to 4pm on weekdays, the floor is nearly empty. Maya wants to fix both problems with better membership tiers.

image.label: Gym with a busy evening and an empty midday
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 헬스장 그림. 왼쪽은 저녁 6시 시계와 붐비는 운동 기구, 오른쪽은 오전 11시 시계와 텅 빈 기구. 실제 헬스장 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Maya build her tiers?
body: Her members use the gym very differently, but most seem happy at $50. Which plan would you choose?

options.text: Basic $30 (gym floor only), Plus $50 (adds classes), Premium $90 (adds towels, a locker and guest passes)
options.feedback: This is **good, better, best**: light users can pay less, heavy users can pay for more, and today's $50 becomes the comfortable middle choice.

options.text: Two tiers: $40 and $60, with the same access but a free T-shirt at $60
options.feedback: It adds choice, but the tiers differ in something few members value. Heavy users have no real reason to pay more.

options.text: Cut the single price to $35 to attract more members
options.feedback: It may bring new members, but every current member now pays $15 less, including the daily user who was happy at $50.

cards.title: Each step up adds what heavier users value.
body: Maya sorts features by who cares about them most:
list: **Basic $30:** gym floor, any time. Real value, but no classes.
**Plus $50:** adds group classes, the thing regulars ask about most.
**Premium $90:** adds towels, a locker and two guest passes a month.
cards.callout: The basic tier must be good enough to buy, but missing something the middle tier clearly has.
cards.softwareNote: Software plans follow the same rule. The cheapest plan should solve a real problem, while the features that matter most to heavy users sit one step up.

cards.title: Filling the empty weekday hours
body: Students, shift workers and people working from home tell Maya that $30 is too much. They are free during the day, when the gym sits empty.
How can she offer them less without her $50 members switching?

options.text: An Off-Peak tier at $20, with entry only from 10am to 4pm on weekdays
options.feedback: This is **price discrimination** with a fence. Most full-price members work during those hours, so they won't cross it, and the empty floor costs Maya almost nothing to fill.

options.text: 20% off any tier with a student ID
options.feedback: The ID is a solid fence, but it only reaches one group. Shift workers and people at home are left out, and the empty hours stay empty.

options.text: A $20 discount code posted on social media
options.feedback: It may bring in new people, but there is no fence. Anyone, including current $50 members, can use it.

cards.title: The fence does the real work.
body: **Price discrimination** means charging different customers different prices for nearly the same thing. It only works with a **fence**: a rule that the customers you charge more won't bother to cross.

Maya's fence is time. A worker who can only train at 7pm gains nothing from an Off-Peak tier. A student with free afternoons does. Each person picks the price that fits their life, and Maya never has to ask what they can afford.

cards.title: A restaurant uses both ideas at once.
body: A bistro offers a two-course, three-course and five-course set menu. That's good, better, best. The three-course menu is built to be the obvious choice.

It also runs an early-dinner menu from 5pm to 6:30pm at a lower price. The fence is the clock. Couples who want a table at 8pm still pay full price, and seats that would sit empty at 5:30 now earn money.

image.label: Menu with three set courses and an early-dinner clock
image.brief: 식당 메뉴판 일러스트. 왼쪽에 2코스·3코스·5코스 세 칸(가운데 3코스 강조), 오른쪽에 5:00~6:30 시계와 "Early dinner" 라벨. 실제 식당 이름이나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Tiers and fences can leak or confuse.
body: Some members who could train at 11am were paying $50. A few will move down to Off-Peak. That's the cost of the fence. Check that the new members outnumber the ones who trade down.
Promises need capacity too. If Plus sells well but classes are full, members feel cheated. And too many tiers slow people down. Three is usually easier to choose from than six.

cards.title: Now it's booking software for salons.
body: Your app lets salons take appointments online. Everyone pays $40 a month. A solo stylist says it's too expensive. A chain with five locations says it would pay more for extra features.

options.text: Solo $15 (one calendar), Team $40 (up to 10 staff), Multi-location $120 (several sites, shared reports)
options.feedback: **Good, better, best** plus a natural **fence**: team size. A five-site chain can't fit into the solo plan, so the cheap price reaches only the users it was built for.

options.text: Keep $40, but give 50% off to anyone who asks in chat
options.feedback: The solo stylist gets help, but so does anyone who asks. Users learn that complaining lowers the price.

options.text: Three plans that differ only in color themes and support speed
options.feedback: You have tiers, but they don't track what users value. The chain still has no reason to pay more, and the solo stylist still pays for features they don't need.

cards.title: Let customers sort themselves, and fence the cheap price.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Good, better, best** gave each type of member a clear step to choose. **Price discrimination** with a fence opened a lower price for people with free daytime hours, without leaking it to everyone else.
**Try it today:** list your three kinds of customers. For each one, write down what they value most and one rule that would keep a lower price limited to the right group.

image.label: Three tier cards and a small fence
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. Basic·Plus·Premium 카드 세 장이 계단처럼 놓여 있고, 옆에 작은 나무 울타리와 "10am–4pm" 시계 표지판. 로고 없음.
